title: Given a chance, women-led microenterprises uplift Nepali communities & conservation - news - Mongabay
description: Given a chance, women-led microenterprises uplift Nepali communities & conservation  news - Mongabay

full_article:
In Naya Padampur, Nepali women are building livelihoods through microenterprises that earn them income and reduce their dependence on forest products.

Previously, many women ventured into the forest outside of Naya Padampur to fetch firewood, a dangerous task due to the proximity of wild animals such as rhinos and tigers.

Successful women-led microenterprises in Nepal and beyond have provided a symbiosis between land and community, allowing conservation efforts to flourish while acting as a catalyst for women’s empowerment.

Still, many women in Nepal face societal and financial hurdles to building businesses and owning property. See All Key Ideas

NAYA PADAMPUR, Nepal — A spinning wheel whirs on a rooftop in Naya Padampur in south-central Nepal, sending ivory strands of yarn through Bin Maya Gurung’s practiced fingers. Smile lines crinkle at the corners of her eyes as she works. Her limbs move in synchrony with the wheel, both integral parts of the machine that ensures her family’s well-being.

She’s sitting at the top of a building that houses a wool spinning enterprise, which has blossomed in the years since she learned to spin wool in the early 2000s. It’s one of many women-led microenterprises that have sprouted across the country.

The past few decades have seen many women in rural Nepal venture into the business environment for the first time, as governmental regulations and societal norms started to shift. The benefits for women entrepreneurs are significant, with a 2022 study conducted in the Parbat district of Nepal showing that 96% of women involved in microenterprises felt confident in supporting their families with the money they earned.

The microenterprises are also important in another way: They provide an alternative source of income to rural families, lessening their reliance on forest products such as timber.

Successful women-led microenterprises — in Nepal and elsewhere — have provided a symbiosis between land and community, allowing conservation efforts to flourish while acting as a catalyst for local income generation and women’s empowerment.

The growth of these microenterprises in Nepal mirrors a growing global recognition of the benefits of women’s involvement in both forests and enterprise. Many women-led microenterprises harvest non-timber forest products with low impact or even a beneficial impact to forest systems. Others, like the spinning enterprise, lessen a household’s reliance on forest products altogether.

But for many Nepali women, social, financial and regulatory hurdles make it an uphill climb to get these businesses off the ground.

The sign outside the enterprise headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

From the ground up

When Gurung arrived in Naya Padampur, her income source became a risky endeavor.

Gurung, now 73, had been part of a settlement called Padampur, which was located within the boundaries of what is now Chitwan National Park, home to vulnerable and endangered species such as single-horned Asiatic rhinoceroses ( Rhinoceros unicornis ), Bengal tigers ( Panthera tigris tigris ) and gharials ( Gavialis gangeticus ). In the 1990s, the Nepali government ordered the relocation of Padampur residents to a place outside the park — the place that is now Naya (new) Padampur.

Gurung remembers her early days in Naya Padampur well. The area was freshly deforested for the settlement. There were very few resources for the residents, and no irrigation systems for farming. Rhinos came close to their houses and roamed across the area nearby.

Gurung’s main source of income for the family at that time was raksi, a traditional Nepali spirit. In order to make the liquor, she was forced to travel into the forest directly outside of the Naya Padampur settlement to fetch firewood, a process made vastly more dangerous because of the proximity of wild animals such as rhinos and tigers. Gurung faced the possibility of wildlife encounters and attacks on these daily trips.

Women in rural Nepal still face an elevated risk of wildlife attacks because their daily tasks, such as collecting water and firewood, often take them directly to the forest edge. A 2026 study found that while women made up less than half of the total tiger attacks in Nepal from 2010-24, the fatality rate of wildlife attacks on women exceeded 70%, whereas the fatality rate in men was under 50%.

Gurung took that risk every day to bring income home.

Bin Maya Gurung sits in the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

At the time of the relocation, there was a general push toward community forestry and community-centric conservation. Nepal passed the Forest Act in 1993, which allowed community forest groups to take over the management of state-owned national forests in their areas. Today, community forest user groups manage around one-third of total forest cover in Nepal, giving agency back to local communities.

There were also many NGOs providing training and funding for the development of microenterprises in Nepal’s rural communities. Two examples were the U.N. Development Programme’s Micro Enterprise Development Programme and programs from the National Trust for Nature Conservation in Nepal (NTNC), which sought to increase community involvement in conservation and provide workshops for women focused on business literacy and marketable skills.

Around Chitwan, these businesses now focus on everything from elephant grass weaving and soap making to beekeeping and nature guiding. Many of the enterprises utilize non-timber forest products for income, according to a case study by the Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN). These businesses — which can produce eco-friendly products such as bamboo baskets, candles and nettle powder, or products such as coffee and bamboo — can actually benefit the larger ecosystem in many ways, CDKN wrote in their study, as well as stimulating the economy.

“Planting of bamboo, coffee, and broom grass on fallow land has supported soil conservation, while the establishment of a permanent tree nursery by a women’s cooperative has helped prevent soil erosion and landslides,” CDKN wrote.

Gurung saw a future free from her reality at the time. She knew of the NTNC and other NGO workshops, and she’d seen women engaged in wool spinning in other communities. She thought if she could get a workshop together, she could leave behind the dangers of wildlife encounters on her treks to the forest. So she gathered 25 women and contacted the NTNC.

That wool spinning workshop marked the start of Gurung’s business journey, one that has stretched over the past two decades. It’s given her freedom from the risky work she used to undertake and brought a powerful source of revenue to her family. It’s allowed her to finance her grandson’s university education and start three different bank accounts to save up money for her family’s future. And it’s greatly diminished her firewood collecting.

During a spinning workshop Gurung was teaching, she mentored Buddhimaya Ghale, who is now the head of the spinning business, which employs 600 women within the Naya Padampur area and another 300 across Nepal. The women involved in the project make anywhere from 8,000-40,000 Nepalese rupees ($52-$263) per month depending on the amount of time they can devote to the handicrafts. The business also offers trainings in wool spinning.

When women are involved in microenterprises, their social status changes, Ghale said. They are able to assert themselves as decision-makers in the household because they provide income for the family. As they slowly emerge as business leaders, they are able to assert their independence more freely.

Sanjay Chaudhary, co-founder of the Tharu Community Women’s Hand, an organization that provides handicraft and business skills workshops for women in the Indigenous Tharu community in the surrounding Chitwan area, said his wife and sister have both been able to establish themselves as entrepreneurs in the community. They actively voice their opinions in town and at meetings, and it’s led others in the community to perceive them differently.

“They’re more empowered, and they started challenging so many social norms, and it’s very good that they’ve started questioning so many conventional narratives,” Chaudhary said.

Buddhimaya Ghale sits behind her desk at the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

An uphill climb

The stories of successful women entrepreneurs speak for themselves. But despite the economic and social benefits, many women remain on the outskirts.

Ghale said the journey into the workplace is not an easy one for women. In many cases, they first need to persuade their families to support their endeavors. Ghale had to strike out on her own to find work for the first time, since her husband did not approve.

After their struggles in the home, Chaudhary said women often face increased scrutiny due to Nepal’s traditionally masculine business environment. In the process of securing loans or other necessary steps to starting a business, he said women will often be asked where their husband is, or judged based on whether they have a good family.

Another hurdle is property rights, Chaudhary said. Only about 20% of women in rural Nepal own land, according to a 2026 study conducted by the Climate Policy Initiative, which makes providing collateral for the bank extremely difficult.

The government has tried multiple strategies to address this, according to Arjun Chapagain, who works as a sustainable forest management coordinator for the Federation of Community Forestry Users Nepal. Nepal’s new Constitution in 2015 granted equal rights to land ownership for men and women. But Chapagain said the reality has yet to catch up with the new policies.

“Even [in] that case, the people just keep only their name here, but again, the control is with the man,” Chapagain said.

The government has also created specific subsidized loans for women entrepreneurs, Chaudhary said. One example of this is a homeownership loan by Nabil Bank designed specifically for women.

But the same study from the Climate Policy Initiative suggests that these loans are still proving elusive for women. According to their report, 88% of the women surveyed in the study relied on personal savings to start their businesses, and only 56% had accessed formal finance.

“This broadly reflects the cumulative impact of cumbersome application processes, stringent evaluation criteria, lack of guarantors, limited advisory support, geographic constraints, and gender bias—particularly for smaller enterprises,” the authors wrote.

And in order to access business loans, microenterprises must be formally registered. A 2026 World Bank Group report evaluating the benefits of formalization found that for about 78% of informal microenterprises, the costs accrued for formal microenterprises would outweigh the benefits of formalization. The Kathmandu Post reported statistics from the Nepal Department of Industry showing that the rate of new registrations for microenterprises has plummeted nearly 75% in five years.

Without scale-specific interventions, the World Bank argues it will be difficult for these enterprises to reach their true growth potential — instead remaining a subsistence income to keep families afloat.

A spinning wheel sits on a table inside the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

Enterprise and conservation

Yet Chaudhary said prioritizing these enterprises may be the key to getting reluctant communities on board with new environmental regulations. Living in Chitwan’s buffer zones, such as Chaudhary’s home in Sauhara, comes with heavy restrictions on fishing, hunting and collecting firewood. At the moment, he said his community has quite a bit of negative sentiment toward conservation due to those restrictions.

“If the park administrations could promote or motivate women for forest-based … enterprises, then that could be the biggest strength,” Chaudhary said. “That could help to make the mindset or narratives positive.”

In addition to the societal benefits, enterprises such the elephant grass handicrafts taught at the Tharu Community Women’s Hand use forest resources highly efficiently, Chaudhary said, with minimal impact on the landscape. Instead of chopping timber, the women simply harvest grasses for their handicrafts, and a small amount of grass can go a long way. Their organization also collaborates with local mahouts, or elephant handlers, Chaudbury said. The mahouts harvest elephant grasses for the microenterprise trainings on their regular forest patrols, so women do not need to make the risky journey into the forest.

After years of wool spinning, Gurung said she rarely visits the forest. Her livelihood no longer relies on forest products. She can feel her body start to age and slow down, but her work is something she can continue in her old age.

Gurung set the spinning wheel in motion. Now her legacy runs through each thread of the group’s handicrafts, and wheels across Nepal will spin long after she is gone.

Woven rugs created by the spinning enterprise lean against the wall at the business headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

title: Nepal to help Indonesia develop international-standard mountain guides - Everest Chronicle
description: Nepal to help Indonesia develop international-standard mountain guides  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) and the Indonesian Mountaineering Federation (FMI) have signed an agreement to strengthen cooperation in mountain guiding, mountaineering education, technical training and safety.

The agreement, signed in Kathmandu on Friday by NNMGA President Tul Singh Gurung and FMI President Major General (Retd) Buyung Lalana, aims to promote professional mountain guiding standards and facilitate the exchange of technical expertise between the two organisations.

The partnership aims to improve professional mountain guiding standards, develop skilled human resources and promote international best practices in climbing and mountaineering safety.

“It is a matter of honour for us to enter into an agreement with FMI to assist them in training for international-standard mountaineering courses,” Gurung said.

Established in 2005, the NNMGA has been training professional mountain guides and represents Nepal at the International Federation of Mountain Guides Associations (IFMGA), also known as UIAGM.

Nepal is among only three Asian countries represented in the international federation, alongside Japan and Kyrgyzstan.

IFMGA-certified Nepali guides have conducted mountaineering courses in several Asian countries, both independently and through institutional projects.

The agreement marks a major international collaborative initiative for the NNMGA, which said it hoped to establish a long-term partnership with Indonesia through technical training, capacity building and mountaineering education programmes tailored to the needs of both countries.

The Indonesian delegation included FMI Deputy President Brigadier General Sandy Muchjitin Latef, General Secretary Dr M Iqbal El Mubarak and Deputy General Secretary Colonel Arief Rehman Haleim. Upendra Ghimire, Indonesia's honorary vice-consul in Nepal, also attended the ceremony.

The NNMGA delegation included immediate past president Ang Norbu Sherpa, Vice-President Lakpa Sherpa, General Secretary Pimba Tenjing Lama, Treasurer Abiral Rai and members of its executive board, technical committee and senior instructors.

In a joint statement, the organisations said they intended to build a long-term partnership to advance mountaineering education, improve safety standards and facilitate the exchange of technical expertise.

The cooperation could also open opportunities for Nepali mountain guides to contribute to mountaineering development in Indonesia, home to Carstensz Pyramid, a 4,884-metre peak in Papua and the highest mountain in Oceania.

Carstensz Pyramid is one of the Seven Summits, the highest mountains on each of the world's seven continents, and attracts climbers seeking to complete the mountaineering challenge. Nepali guides also lead expeditions to the peak.

title: Nepal’s U.N. Envoy Meets Guterres, Thanks U.N. for Flood Aid and Calls for Stronger Climate Action - nepyork
description: Nepal’s U.N. Envoy Meets Guterres, Thanks U.N. for Flood Aid and Calls for Stronger Climate Action  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Lok Bahadur Thapa, met Wednesday with U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, praising his leadership and commitment to multilateralism and thanking the United Nations for its assistance following devastating floods in Nepal.

During the meeting, Thapa commended Guterres’ principled leadership, commitment to multilateralism and efforts to promote international solidarity and ensure no one is left behind, according to a statement from the Nepali envoy.

Thapa reaffirmed Nepal’s commitment to the U.N. Charter, multilateral cooperation and collective action to address global challenges. He also expressed appreciation for assistance from the U.N. system following recent climate-related disasters in Nepal.

Guterres expressed condolences for the loss of lives and property caused by the disasters and acknowledged Nepal’s active role in advancing multilateral cooperation, according to the statement.

Economic and Social Council, chairmanship of the group of least developed countries, facilitation of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development and chairmanship of the U.N. General Assembly’s First Committee.

He also praised Nepal’s advocacy for climate action and its longstanding contributions to international peace and security as one of the leading contributors of troops and police personnel to U.N. peacekeeping missions.

Recalling his visit to the base camp of Mount Everest three years ago, Guterres highlighted the devastating effects of climate change in the Himalayas and stressed the need for urgent and ambitious global climate action, the statement said.

Both sides emphasized the importance of strengthening early warning systems, improving resilience to climate-related disasters and promoting greater international solidarity and cooperation to advance global climate goals.

title: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 30: Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, has said that the crises caused by climate change in the Himalayan region are not confined within the geographical boundaries of just one country.

At a high-level regional dialogue organized on Thursday in Bangkok by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and the Government of Nepal under the title 'From Everest to the Sea,' he said that global cooperation is necessary for mountain conservation.

Minister Shrestha's secretariat has stated that representatives from 53 countries have supported the four proposals that Nepal presented to the international community to reduce the impacts of climate change and manage cross-border disaster risks.

Nepal has emphasized the need to develop a multi-hazard early warning system based on satellites, artificial intelligence (AI), and modern technology, through collaboration between international space agencies, scientific institutions, and the government, to monitor risky mountain slopes and glaciers.

Minister Shrestha also mentioned that Prime Minister Balendra Shah proposed the 'Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism' for coordinating information exchange, glacier monitoring, and early warning systems in the Himalayan region.

Minister Shrestha emphasized that immediate financial assistance should be made available for disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and recovery, and that it should be accessible and grant-based.

He said that in high Himalayan areas, monitoring and early warning should be supported through grants, not loans, and investments in riverside hydropower projects to border towns should be managed by considering the risks from the source to the sea.((RSS)

title: When There Is No Home to Return To: Nepal and the Future of Climate Migration - Human Rights First
description: When There Is No Home to Return To: Nepal and the Future of Climate Migration  Human Rights First
publisher.title: Human Rights First
full_article:
By Emily Suu Myatnoe (Communications Intern)

Madhav Ghimire still carries the keys to his home. For years, those keys opened the door to the six-room house he shared with his partner in Devighat, Nepal. Then, on August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flood tore through communities along the Trishuli River after part of the Langtang Lirung glacier collapsed near Nepal's border with China's Tibet region. When Ghimire returned, the landscape had changed so dramatically that he could no longer tell where his house once stood.

He kept the keys anyway.

“Though I lost everything, I have still carried the keys of my home,” Ghimire told Reuters. “It gives me a sense that I have everything.”

His story captures something that statistics about climate displacement can struggle to convey, that displacement is not simply movement from one place to another. It often means losing a home, a livelihood, a community, and the expectation that there will eventually be somewhere familiar to return.

In Betrawati, another community in Nepal devastated by the flood, survivors returned to what Reuters described as an expanse of gray silt. Homes, businesses, farmland, and pieces of everyday life had disappeared beneath mud and debris. By September 18, at least 1,386 people had been killed in Nepal and more than 5,100 remained missing.

Scientists are still studying precisely what caused the collapse. Researchers with World Weather Attribution found that human-caused climate change helped create conditions that made the disaster more likely, including glacier thinning and thawing permafrost. Average temperatures in the Himalayan region were around 5 degrees Celsius above normal during August, with researchers attributing about 1.5 degrees of that increase to climate change.

But what happens after a climate disaster makes home unlivable?

Most people displaced by climate impacts remain within their own countries or move elsewhere in their region. But for those who need to cross an international border to find safety, another problem emerges: the legal framework for seeking asylum was largely built without climate displacement in mind.

A September 2026 report from the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP) examines this growing protection gap. The report notes that while most climate displacement happens internally, people who are displaced internationally by climate events face limited opportunities to reach another country through safe, lawful pathways. Many destination countries still lack policy frameworks designed to respond specifically to climate-related migration.

Even the language we use reveals the problem. Terms such as “climate refugee” may sound intuitive, but refugee status carries a specific legal meaning outlined in the 1951 Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocols. Climate-related displacement does not, by itself, necessarily fit within the existing protection framework, which was created in the aftermath of the horror of World War II, at a time when climate change was not yet a driving factor of forced migration..

IRAP's research suggests that policymakers should avoid allowing the search for a perfect definition to become an obstacle to helping people affected by climate change. Instead, experts interviewed for the report emphasized identifying people's actual protection needs and using independent socio-environmental data to determine eligibility for potential pathways. This distinction matters because people do not experience displacement in neat categories. A climate disaster may destroy someone's livelihood while existing political persecution, gender-based violence, poverty, disability, or other vulnerabilities shape whether they can safely remain, relocate internally, or cross a border.

I was thinking about that complexity on September 24, when I attended “(Re)Setting a U.S. Policy for Climate Mobility,” a Climate Week NYC roundtable bringing together advocates and policy experts to consider how the United States could expand legal protections for climate-displaced people seeking safety and permanence. Eleanor Acer, Senior Director of Global Humanitarian Protection at Human Rights First, joined experts from organizations including IRAP, Refugees International, Haitian Bridge Alliance, the Migration Policy Institute, and others. One theme returned throughout the discussion: a meaningful response to climate mobility cannot exist in a single policy silo.

Climate displacement is simultaneously international and domestic. It intersects with immigration, housing, food insecurity, economic inequality, gender-based violence, disaster response, and human rights. Addressing it therefore requires communication not only between governments, but also across agencies, sectors, advocates, and the communities most directly affected. Acer emphasized the need to think both internationally and nationally, and both internally and across borders. Rather than relying on one immigration mechanism, she discussed the importance of a more comprehensive protection system—one that strengthens Temporary Protected Status, creates additional pathways to safety and permanence, respects non-refoulement protections against returning people to danger, and protects family unity.

Her comments also pointed toward a fundamental limitation in today's system: there is no single international treaty creating comprehensive migration pathways specifically for people displaced by climate impacts. That leaves policymakers with a difficult question: How can we be visionary about what protection should look like while still creating solutions that can actually be implemented?

IRAP’s report examines the Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union, which created a dedicated mobility pathway for citizens of Tuvalu without requiring individual applicants to prove that climate change personally displaced them. But IRAP cautions that such a model is most workable under relatively narrow circumstances. That lesson is particularly important because not being explicitly excluded does not necessarily mean being meaningfully included.

IRAP also considers adapting existing labor pathways, which may offer more politically feasible and scalable opportunities for climate-affected people. Yet the report warns that labor migration programs themselves can expose workers to rights violations, meaning expansion must be accompanied by safeguards that protect the people those programs are intended to serve.

The September roundtable similarly explored the possibility of beginning where progress is achievable: at state and local levels, across existing sectors, and through policies that can demonstrate what works before being expanded. Participants discussed the need for stronger communication across government, accessible terminology and public education, and new coalitions capable of connecting work that may already be happening separately. Most importantly, any system designed around climate mobility must center the autonomy and experiences of people affected by it. Climate-displaced people are more than moving numbers, and their circumstances, reasons for moving, vulnerabilities, families, and hopes for the future differ.

Climate mobility will require difficult conversations about borders, responsibility, resources, and who receives protection. Those conversations are particularly significant for countries like the United States, which has historically contributed a substantial share of global carbon emissions while possessing resources that many climate-vulnerable countries do not.

But perhaps the first step is changing how we understand displacement itself.

A home is the land a family expected to rebuild on, the school their children attended, the work that supported them, and the community that surrounded them. After Nepal's 2015 earthquake, families in the Trishuli River region endured tremendous destruction, but some survivors told Reuters that they could at least return to their land and rebuild. After August's flood, that possibility disappeared for many. One teacher who lost two houses and saw her farmland buried under debris described the difference simply: “This time, we have lost everything.”

No migration policy can restore what the flood took from those families. But as climate change increasingly reshapes where people can safely live, human rights protections can help determine what happens next. The question is no longer only how governments respond when disaster strikes. It is whether people forced to leave will have meaningful choices about where they can go, whether their families can remain together, and whether safety can become something more permanent.

Ghimire still has the keys to a house he may never find again. The future of climate mobility will depend, in part, on whether losing a home also means losing the right to find another.

Cold Chain Support in Chad, Surgical Training in Ukraine, and Medical Care in Flood-Affected Nepal

By Tori Gordon

Over the past week, Direct Relief sent 380 shipments of requested medical aid, containing 10.2 million defined daily doses of medication, to organizations across 41 U.S. states and territories and 26 other countries.

Shipments sent this week included cystic fibrosis medications, cancer therapies, diabetes treatments, and cold-chain equipment.

Strengthening Cold Chain Across Chad's Provinces

Chad's Directorate General of Pharmacy, Medicines and Laboratories received 23 refrigerators from Direct Relief, one for each of the country's provincial pharmaceutical supply centers, during a ceremony presided over by the Minister of Public Health and Prevention.

The donation supports a broader effort to modernize the country's cold chain and ensure the safe storage of temperature-sensitive medicines in even the most remote provinces, following a separate Direct Relief-funded cold room recently completed at the Central Pharmaceutical Supply Agency in N'Djamena.

The investment builds on Direct Relief's partnership with Chad's Ministry of Public Health, established in 2024, which has grown to include 43 shipments of medical aid, from midwife kits supporting maternal health to emergency response following cholera outbreaks and flooding. The ministry also recently received its first shipment of HPV vaccines as part of its expanding preventive care efforts.

"Strengthening the cold chain is an essential link in our ambition to build a more efficient, resilient and equitable pharmaceutical supply system for the benefit of the entire Chadian population," said Dr. Ayoub Moussa Abderaman, Director General of Pharmacy, Medicines and Laboratories.

Surgical Training Builds Reconstructive Care Capacity in Ukraine

The Penn Center for Global Health's Ukraine Reconstruction Program, supported by Direct Relief, recently completed an in-country surgical training mission in Mukachevo, Ukraine. The mission brought together an international team of reconstructive surgeons to advance local expertise in treating complex combat-related extremity injuries. Working alongside Ukrainian colleagues, the team provided hands-on training in advanced soft tissue reconstruction and frame fixation while treating patients with severe combat injuries.

Training surgeons within their own clinical environment helps build a sustainable, locally led system of reconstructive care and reduces the need for patients to travel abroad for specialized treatment.

"Our goal is not simply to perform operations during each mission, but to equip Ukrainian surgical teams with the knowledge, technical skills, and confidence to independently manage increasingly complex injuries long after our visiting teams have departed," the program said.

Free Medical and Dental Camp Reaches Flood-Affected Community in Nepal

Mountain Heart Nepal, in collaboration with the Rasuwa Nuwakot Tourism Society, supported a free medical and dental camp in Ward No. 6, Dhunche, Rasuwa, benefiting communities affected by recent floods and landslides. Approximately 200 patients received care, including general health exams, dental checkups and treatment, and free essential medicines, with particular attention given to those requiring regular medication for chronic conditions whose access to care had been disrupted by the disaster.

Direct Relief and Friends of Mountain Heart Nepal provided the essential medicines and medical supplies that supported the camp, as the organization continues working to ensure continuity of care for people with chronic illnesses and those in geographically challenging areas.

title: Nepal to push dedicated mountain agenda - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal to push dedicated mountain agenda  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 31: Nepal is preparing to formally propose a dedicated mountain agenda at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), following consultations with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Under a joint initiative with Bhutan, Nepal plans to submit the proposal to the UNFCCC Secretariat and the COP31 Presidency.

The country is seeking regular high-level mountain dialogues, a dedicated mountain work programme and the inclusion of the specific risks faced by mountain regions in the global climate framework, according to the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment.

Nepal has warned that a temporary rise in global temperatures above the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold, known as temperature overshoot, would accelerate glacier melting, destabilise mountain ecosystems and increase risks to water, food, energy and livelihoods.

Called for grant-based funding

Nepal has also highlighted the need for substantial climate finance to address the impacts of climate-related disasters and support recovery and reconstruction, the Ministry said.

According to preliminary estimates presented at the Climate Summit organised ahead of the COP 31 on Thursday, around US$ 4.7 billion may be required for recovery and reconstruction following the August Bhotekoshi disaster. This is equivalent to nearly 10 per cent of Nepal's gross domestic product (GDP).

Nepal's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) estimates that the country will require US$ 18 to 20 billion in adaptation finance for the period from 2025 to 2035.

Nepal is calling for easier access to climate finance, predictable and grant-based funding, faster disbursement, new and additional resources for addressing loss and damage, technology transfer and capacity development, the Ministry said.

Despite contributing less than 0.1 per cent of global emissions, Nepal faces a disproportionately high burden of climate-related damage. The country maintains that nations with greater historical responsibility for emissions and stronger financial capacity should support a just recovery without increasing the debt burden of vulnerable countries.

Progress in accessing climate finance

Nepal has made progress in securing international climate finance through various funding mechanisms.

Over the past two years, Nepal has submitted more than 17 proposals worth around US$ 170 million to the Adaptation Fund. Six proposals have received approval at different stages, with some fully approved, some under implementation and others at the stage of preparing detailed proposals.

Similarly, Nepal has secured around US$ 157 million through six projects under the Green Climate Fund (GCF), most of which are under implementation.

The National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC) has also secured USD 9.2 million for a project focused on climate-vulnerable areas of Karnali.

Australia pledges for support

Australia has highlighted its support for Nepal through a US$ 20 million humanitarian assistance appeal and a US$ 15 million investment through the HARIT programme. The HARIT programme aims to promote locally led climate adaptation, strengthen the capacity of local institutions and improve the resilience of vulnerable communities.

Australia has also stressed the need for urgent action to keep the global temperature rise within the 1.5 degrees Celsius target.

Nepal, meanwhile, is highlighting the connections between mountains, rivers, oceans and vulnerable communities through its 'Sagarmatha to the Sea' concept.

According to the Ministry, Nepal is advancing its NDC 3.0, mountain strategy and other climate-related policy documents while emphasising the meaningful participation of women, children, young and indigenous people, persons with disabilities and marginalised communities in climate action.

title: Unified command key to effective disaster response: Nepali Army - The Rising Nepal
description: Unified command key to effective disaster response: Nepali Army  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 31: The Nepali Army has called for a unified chain of command in disaster management, saying overlapping responsibilities and lengthy decision-making have hampered coordination and delayed rescue operations.

Briefing a parliamentary special committee formed to study and monitor disasters along the Bhotekoshi and Budhigandaki corridors under the House of Representatives on Friday, Brigadier General Subash Jung Thapa said unclear responsibilities had created significant challenges during the recent Bhotekoshi and Budhigandaki floods.

He said a unified command structure was essential for the swift mobilisation of security personnel, equipment and other resources during disasters.

Sharing details of the Budhigandaki flood in northern Gorkha, Thapa said an avalanche from Siringe Himal had blocked the Syar Khola, a tributary of the Budhigandaki River, for nearly two hours before the water broke through at 6:15 am. The flood reached Chitwan via Arughat, Bensighat and Mugling within around eight hours. The disaster damaged the under-construction 341-megawatt Budhigandaki Hydropower Project, swept away six bridges and disrupted 91.5 kilometres of roads. Six people remain missing.

The Army launched aerial reconnaissance at 6:36 am and began search and rescue operations after reaching Gorkha at 7:52 am. During the six-day operation, it rescued 1,025 people and transported 13,930 kilogrammes of relief materials. It also assisted foreign tourists along the Manaslu trekking route and reconstructed a Bailey bridge at Arughat to restore connectivity.

Presenting recommendations for improving disaster preparedness, the Army called for establishing emergency operation centres in all seven provinces and maintaining specialised search and rescue teams for immediate deployment.

It also recommended increasing the availability of large, medium and small helicopters, improving information systems, ensuring adequate rescue equipment and enlarging the pool of trained personnel.

Thapa said inadequate equipment and trained human resources had created difficulties during rescue operations following the Bhotekoshi flood.

Eleven hydropower plants in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were damaged, with floodwaters entering the tunnels of six projects and extending five kilometres or more.

The Army has deployed 42 personnel in the affected areas, and search operations will continue until the tunnels are fully inspected. It has rescued 4,220 people so far, including 3,243 within 96 hours of the Bhotekoshi flood.

The Army also recommended that district disaster management committees lead post-disaster recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction under the supervision of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). It warned that at least 45 glacial lakes on the Nepali side of the Himalayas were at risk of bursting and called for expanding early warning systems to the household level.

Chief of the Army Staff (CoAS) General Ashok Raj Sigdel also pointed out weaknesses in the existing disaster response mechanism, describing the chain of command as unnecessarily lengthy and cumbersome.

He said the National Emergency Operations Centre (NEOC), established after the 2015 earthquake, required substantial restructuring to improve its effectiveness. Recent floods, landslides and tunnel accidents had exposed shortcomings in the country's disaster management framework, he added.

General Sigdel stressed the need to continue search operations, clearly define agencies' responsibilities during debris removal and prioritise roads, health services and educational institutions during reconstruction. He also called for proper management of recovered bodies and stronger early warning systems against glacial lake outbursts and avalanches.

Meanwhile, Inspector General of Nepal Police Dan Bahadur Karki informed the committee that 112 bodies recovered following the floods and landslides along the Bhotekoshi and Budhigandaki corridors had been identified and handed over to their families.

Police had launched a special 'Timure to Triveni' operation along both riverbanks, covering the stretch from Timure in Rasuwa to Triveni in Nawalparasi, to trace bodies swept downstream.

Govinda Puri, chief of the Nepal Police Disaster Rescue and Coordination Information Management Centre, said DNA profiling had been completed for 3,498 people using samples collected from relatives of those killed or missing in the disasters.

The Armed Police Force (APF) also called for the immediate activation of all thematic clusters to make disaster response more effective and allow security agencies to focus primarily on search and rescue operations.

APF Deputy Inspector General Krishna Dhakal said a trilateral early warning mechanism involving China, Nepal and India was necessary to minimise the impact of cross-border disasters such as the Bhotekoshi flood. He stressed real-time information sharing among the three countries to ensure warnings could be transmitted within minutes or seconds.

The security agencies collectively called for clearer responsibilities, stronger inter-agency coordination, improved rescue capacity and an efficient command structure to strengthen the country's disaster preparedness.

title: Nepal-India agree to strengthen border security - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal-India agree to strengthen border security  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter,Kathmandu, Oct. 31: Nepal and India have agreed to strengthen border security, enhance technology-based border management and intensify bilateral cooperation to curb cross-border crimes and illegal activities.

The agreement was reached at the 3-day 10th Nepal-India Coordination meeting, which concluded on Friday in Kathmandu under the leadership of Nepal's Armed Police Force (APF) Inspector General Narayan Dutta Paudyal and India's Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) Director General Sanjay Singhal.

According to APF Nepal Deputy Inspector General (DIG) and Spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki, the meeting reviewed progress on the decisions made during the ninth coordination meeting and expressed a joint commitment to strengthen cooperation at strategic, operational and field levels.

Both sides agreed to enhance timely information sharing and coordination among security agencies to control illegal activities and cross-border crimes.

Senior APF Nepal officials and representatives from the Ministries of Foreign Affairs and Home Affairs, the Department of Survey, Nepal Police, and the National Investigation Department attended the meeting. The Indian delegation included senior SSB officials and representatives from the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu and the Indian Ministries of External Affairs and Home Affairs.

The two sides appreciated the professionalism and cooperation demonstrated by APF Nepal and SSB units in maintaining peace and security along the Nepal–India border.

They also agreed to strengthen institutional cooperation to address security and social harmony challenges arising from the misuse of social media and the spread of misinformation.

In order to manage the no-man’s-land (Dasgaja) area effectively, both sides agreed to continue joint efforts to remove unauthorised cultivation, encroachments and illegal structures. They also agreed to strengthen field-level coordination for the regular maintenance, repair and reconstruction of border pillars in accordance with the decisions of the Boundary Working Group (BWG) and the Survey Officials Committee (SOC).

The meeting also agreed to strengthen the timely exchange of information to combat transnational criminal networks, illegal trafficking, human trafficking, counterfeit currency and drug smuggling, as well as the unauthorised movement of third-country nationals.

Both sides agreed to tighten security checks and document verification at border points to prevent the illegal entry of third-country nationals through the open border. They also agreed to conduct coordinated patrols along the no-man’s-land and immediately share information about suspicious individuals.

The two sides further agreed to expand the use of modern technology and specialised training to address emerging border security challenges and strengthen institutional ties through regular exchange visits between the two security forces.

Discussions were also held on transforming the traditional border security system into a modern, technology-enabled smart border management system. Proposals included installing CCTV cameras to monitor the no-man’s-land, placing luggage scanners and walk-through metal detectors at major border crossings, and expanding the use of drones within their respective territories.

The meeting also discussed organising a joint swift-water rescue exercise at the APF Nepal Disaster Management Training School in Kurintar, Chitwan, to enhance preparedness for natural disasters, including floods, landslides and earthquakes.

To facilitate legitimate travellers, both sides agreed to expand help desks at border points. They also agreed to organise friendly sports events and joint cultural programmes on international observance days and major festivals to promote mutual trust and goodwill.

The bilateral coordination meeting between APF Nepal and India’s Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) has been held alternately in the two countries since 2012. The next meeting will be held in India next year, Karki said.

title: 302 ropanis of public land comes under govt ownership - The Rising Nepal
description: 302 ropanis of public land comes under govt ownership  The Rising Nepal

By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 31: A total of 302 ropanis of land in seven wards of Kathmandu Metropolitan City (KMC) have been transferred to the Nepal government under the implementation of the 2052 BS report of the Rawal Commission.

The Land Revenue Office, Dillibazaar, has transferred the land to the name of the Nepal Government by deducting the areas identified as encroached upon in the Rawal Commission's report. The land is located in KMC wards 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 29.

The committee formed to implement the report by the Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration has begun the process of transferring government and public land identified as encroached upon to the government's ownership.

Under the process, the areas identified as encroached upon are being deducted in a consolidated manner from the respective land parcels and registered in the name of the Nepal government, according to the Secretariat of the Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration, Pratibha Rawal.

A committee has been formed under the coordination of Chief Survey Officer Ramesh Gyawali to oversee the implementation of the report.

The committee comprises under-secretaries from the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, chiefs of the concerned land revenue and survey offices, the chief of the Local Level Coordination Section, a section officer from the Department of Land Management and Archive and a survey officer from the Department of Survey as member-secretary.

The Rawal Commission had submitted its report in 2052 B.S. after studying the status of government and public land across the country. It had recommended measures to protect such land, including government and public land encroached upon or registered in the names of private individuals.

The Ministry has now initiated the implementation of the report after a prolonged delay, beginning the process of bringing the identified government and public land under government ownership.

title: In Nepal, police take three journalists in for questioning — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, police take three journalists in for questioning — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, plainclothes police officers visited the offices of several media outlets, took three journalists in for questioning and attempted to detain other media workers. As Kathmandu Post reports, law enforcement officers were likely trying to identify the sources of publications about police leadership and an investigation involving Inam Sapkota.

On Friday, police took Bishwamani Subedi of Nepal Press, Motive News editor Shobharaj Baral, and DNA Khabar editor-in-chief Dhiraj Basnet in for questioning. At the office of Naya Patrika Daily, police officers tried for nearly three hours to take journalist Navaraj Mainali away, but left the premises after protests. Law enforcement officers also came to the Diyo Post office in Kathmandu, but did not find editor-in-chief Sudip Bishwakarma there.

Questions about publication sources

Nepal Press editor-in-chief Matrika Poudel said police asked about the grounds, facts, evidence and sources of the published materials. According to him, the journalists replied that they could provide such information to a competent court or the Press Council Nepal. Poudel also said the officers asked why the outlet was “spreading negativity” and mentioned a publication about alleged pressure on Inspector General of Police Dan Bahadur Karki to resign.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Deepak Raj Awasthi, a representative of Nepal Police's Cyber Bureau, denied that journalists had been arrested and said three people had been summoned to provide explanations. After protests, everyone taken to the police station was released the same evening.

Reaction from media and authorities

The Federation of Nepali Journalists called the police actions an attack on press freedom. Its president, Nirmala Sharma, said using police against the media violates freedom of speech and the constitution. Former federation head Shiva Gaunle compared the police attempts to identify the sources of journalistic materials with practices from the era of the autocratic rule of King Gyanendra Shah.

The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party also condemned the police actions, stating that complaints about media materials should be considered by the institutions designated for that purpose. The Prime Minister's Office said that the prime minister, his secretariat and his office had not been informed of the operation in advance. After receiving the information, the prime minister instructed that the journalists be released and that police not enter newsrooms. The Press Council Nepal said police officers had not explained the grounds for the detentions and had not shown arrest warrants.

title: Amber Alert for the Red Panda - Nepali Times
description: Amber Alert for the Red Panda  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Which panda came first: the Giant Panda in China or the Red Panda in Nepal?

Although the Giant Panda is better known worldwide, the Red Panda was first described by Western scientists in 1825 and given the scientific name Ailurus fulgens . It took another 50 years for the Giant Panda to be scientifically classified even though it is now the celebrity mammal in zoos across the world.

After DNA analysis concluded that the giant panda was actually from the Ursidae bear family, scientists found out that the red panda belonged to a unique taxonomical family called Ailuridae , closer to raccoons and squirrels.

The name ‘panda’ is actually derived from words in a dialect in eastern Nepal ‘nigalya panja’ which means ‘bamboo paw’. Although scientists have studied this shy and elusive mammal for 200 years, very little is still known about its habits and habitat on the forest canopy.

There are said to be only about 1,000 red pandas in Nepal, most of them in the lush cloud forests of eastern Nepal where the thin bamboo called nigalo grows in an altitude belt between 2,400m-3,900m. Although the panda is a carnivore, its favourite snack is bamboo shoots.

Nepali scientists are making progress studying the behaviour of the red panda from a research centre in Taplejung. The findings are important because the mammal is an indicator species that points to the health of the forest ecosystem where it lives.

“Nepal has been successful in receiving global funding but there is a need for a more systematic research method,” says

Anusha Pahari of Red Panda Network, which organised an inaugural Red Panda Symposium 2026 in collaboration with Rotterdam Zoo, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and the AZA SAFE Red Panda Program earlier this month in Kathmandu.

Protecting the red panda means safeguarding the forest ecosystem on which the animal depends, and working with the communities where the animals roam.

Besides habitat fragmentation and disturbance from new infrastructure, red pandas are also poached and traded for their fur. Disease adds another threat.

Conservationists at the Kathmandu symposium emphasised that protecting the animal means addressing these pressures together, rather than treating forest loss, wildlife trade, and disease as separate problems.

“Fragmented habitats is a major threat for red pandas, and there is an urgent need to identify potential corridors and increase connectivity and water sources so that their population is not affected,” explains Damber Bista of Red Panda Network.

Funding for nature conservation work worldwide is shrinking, and this has also affected resources for research into red pandas. Experts say the challenge is not simply to launch conservation activities, but to keep them going and connect research with work on the ground.

Many rural households across the red panda range from Taplejung to Dolpo in Nepal depend on community forests for their livelihood. Conservation must therefore extend beyond protected areas into landscapes shared by people and wildlife.

“Habitat fragmentation could affect the genetic diversity of

red pandas, and this means we have to be extra careful that human-induced activities do not affect them,” says Pahari.

Another threat for red pandas is from feral dogs which can transmit rabies, and conservation activity has included vaccinating over 10,000 free-ranging community dogs in rural Nepal.

CHARISMATIC SPECIES

Estimates for the red panda population in Nepal have varied widely, researchers have analysed faecal samples to estimate the population which has increased over the years to about 1,000 after the animals were also found in Bhojpur, and as far west as Dolpo. Scientists have also catalogued 72 bamboo species which the pandas eat.

Research gaps remain, however, especially in western Nepal. There is also limited awareness of the animal’s conservation needs. The range of population estimates highlights why a clearer picture matters. Surveys help establish where red pandas live, and spread awareness beyond them just being a charismatic species.

“There is growing awareness for wildlife conservation, but most of it goes to saving larger species like tigers and wild elephants, overshadowing small mammals such as the red panda,” says Pahari.

For communities living alongside red pandas, conservation starts in the forests that sustain their livelihoods and shelter wildlife. Ecotourism and habitat restoration offer ways to connect protection with local livelihoods, giving communities a stake in the animal’s future.

“Close engagement with the community is vital for awareness and conservation, not just for red pandas but nature conservation overall. Local stewardship is the only way in Nepal where people live in close proximity to wildlife,” says Nishan KC from WWF Nepal, which also works in cross-border collaboration since the red panda habitat spans Nepal to India and China.

The red panda’s future is tied to the forests and to the people who depend on them. Giving communities the knowledge and resources to protect that shared home is essential to helping people and red pandas coexist.

Says KC: “Whether it is patrolling for poaching control or any other awareness effort, conservation is something that should happen continuously, it cannot stop.”

title: Solve Hunger Problem - The Rising Nepal
description: Solve Hunger Problem  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Nepal's position on the 2026 Global Hunger Index (GHI) is both an optimistic indicator and a call to action. Ranked 72nd out of 122 countries with a score of 14.5 out of 100, Nepal falls into the moderate category of hunger under the index and ranks better than its South Asian neighbours, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan. Nonetheless, it cannot deny the basic truth about millions who are finding difficulty in securing nutritious food.

Nepal's progress in GHI scores is commendable, as the score of 14.5 in 2026 shows improvement compared to the previous score of 18.4 in 2018. Similarly, the rate of child stunting among children under five years old has decreased from 55.9 per cent in 2000 to 26.2 per cent in 2026. It can be taken as an indicator of the good progress made by Nepal towards reducing hunger and undernutrition.

The four parameters that measure hunger in the GHI include poor caloric consumption, stunted growth among children, child malnutrition, and the death rate among children under five years old. The combination of these four parameters provides an extended explanation of the food security problem rather than the mere availability of food only. Hunger is not merely a condition wherein people lack sufficient food to survive but also includes the absence of adequate nutritional requirements for growth and health.

The decreasing GHI score in Nepal shows how constant work on the country's healthcare, awareness about nutrition, and public services can bear fruit. At the same time, the progress in terms of national indicators does not necessarily mean that each and every household has received positive changes. Poor transportation, low economic conditions, unemployment, poor infrastructure, and inequality in the availability of services can cause some groups of society to lag behind others.

Even more interesting is the comparison between countries within the same region. In terms of the Global Hunger Index, Sri Lanka is placed 53rd at a score of 10.2, Bangladesh is placed 84th, India 100th, and Pakistan 106th. Even though it may seem that the ranking of Nepal is better than those of others, there are several things to consider when discussing rankings.

What seems to be even more worrying is the difference between the global average score (18.1) and that of South Asia (23.5). This average indicates the ongoing problem of hunger and malnutrition in the region despite economic development and advancements in technologies and agricultural production.

The next step towards development in Nepal would be to ensure that the successes on the national level translate into effective improvements in the nutrition of the households. Higher agricultural production is desirable, but the increase in production itself does not guarantee an end to hunger. In addition to increased agricultural productivity, farmers will require improved irrigation facilities, quality seeds, food storage capacity, agricultural credit, proper marketing, and good pricing.

Another priority is the need to ensure affordability of nutritious food. Even when a household consumes adequate calories, there is no guarantee that it receives enough protein, vitamins, and minerals. For this reason, the policies should encourage diversification of foods consumed to include vegetables, fruits, beans, eggs, and other nutritious foods available locally. It is also important to provide school meals, maternal nutritional care, breastfeeding, and treatment of childhood wasting.

Climate change is an added factor here. The occurrence of irregular rains, drought, floods, landslides, and other climatic conditions can affect food production. Hence, it is vital for Nepal to incorporate strategies related to climate-resilient agriculture, irrigation development, crop diversification, and disaster preparedness in its food security plan. Programmes for social protection should include households that are suffering from disruptions to their income and food due to such emergencies.

Lastly, there is a need to emphasise the importance of accountability. It is necessary that governments at various levels keep track of nutritional results and identify areas that are suffering from deprivation. Coordination between various programmes such as agriculture, health, education, and local government is important, as there is no single ministry that can deal with hunger.

Certainly, Nepal deserves some credit for its progress, demonstrated through the reduction of the country’s hunger index and the decline in child stunting levels. However, such a middle-level classification cannot be perceived as an indicator of the success already achieved by Nepal. In fact, the actual indicator of success lies not in the country’s ranking among other countries of the region, but in the ability of every child to develop healthy, free from malnutrition, and every family to have access to sufficient amounts of healthy food at any time of the year.

Consequently, all the achievements of Nepal that have been gained since 2018 should not lead the country to complacency, but should rather be viewed as proof that more can be done.

title: Nepal Needs Light Of Enlightenment - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal Needs Light Of Enlightenment  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Nepal is too diverse in geography, population, economy and political parties. No single perspective can grasp the totality of its entire landscape. Different scales of conversations of leadership with people are essential to their voice and visibility in decision making. The demand of Nepalis for a just political order needs the light of new insights about the condition of living, their needs, aspirations and their rights to boost their freedom and self-worth without mindlessly slipping into the culture of conformism, silence and creeping authoritarianism. To improve the foundational thinking of life, its heritage of wisdom had shaped three lifting phases of enlightenment—pre-religious Vedic, Janak’s spiritual and Buddha’s rationalistic ones. They for long shaped the ecological, social, economic and political worldview and remained relevant to fill the flame of life with ideals for socialisation beyond mundane expediency and rational self-love of leaders.

Nepal’s intellectual tradition has inclined an edifying search for moral engagement where the modern political culture of division of “I” and “we” is abridged by linking with nature, family, society, nationality and humanity. Those living under the low standards of comfort and upset with the false hope of their leaders about the perfection of their living are looking for the warmth of heritage and culture of civic patriotism against economic and geopolitical determinism. The enlightenment deficits of Nepalis have shifted their impulse to personal survival and opportunity. It is opening sharp contradictions within political parties and civil society over values, institutions, articulation and succession and trapping them in a habit-driven mode, not norm-governed action.

Intellectual potential

Unaware of the nation’s intellectual and resource potential to fulfill necessities of life, Nepalis buy their subsistence from abroad. The survival uprooting of people shows external reliance on what BP Koirala calls bhui phutta barga (comprador class) who no longer care about the loss of the ability of the nation and people to determine its politics—domestic and foreign. The execution of the blue economy of monetization has razed production structures and broke its links with agriculture and ecology. Lure to cloud capitalism driven by hi-tech web can only hack the welfare leap of the Nepali state and deform its polity. Nepalis now seek to flee from the empty life riddled with data vanity to find the light of enlightenment.

Certain caveats are vital: Shifting politics from a game of winning to serving: So far what counted in Nepali politics, like sport, is winning through the use of passion to support one’s own political party or leaders than apply universal reason that transcends affno manchhe (clients) to rationally include all people. Party cadres accept the life of subordination to leaders for favour, not articulation of popular interests and policies, even if they act against national interests. The Supreme Court has to discipline them for their unlawful conduct. The dynamics of the information revolution is upending the hitherto sparkling ideological justification of what they do by encouraging Nepalis to wriggle out of this stasis and move to a self-chosen path to acquire alertness, courage, maturity and dignity, the sources of enlightenment.

A common response to shared national and geopolitical situations can widen the frame of politics beyond the zone of a zero-sum game of “friend” and “foe” and craft policies and laws to address the new stratification of society by knowledge, communication and technology and new challenges of climate change. Widening of opportunity bolsters the institutional muscle of the Nepali state, enabling it to address the crisis of existence so that youths do not have to migrate abroad for livelihood. It deprives the nation of dynamic force for production and transformation and stifles the posterity to enjoy the products of their own labour.

Nepali leaders did not lack the means of releasing intense passion and flashy speeches on national issues. But they amount to only a sound bite. An awareness of the persistence of its soft power of spiritualism, wisdom, nerve and dexterity to settle problems is vital for people to relish a life of dignity, not instrumentalised by generation, class, market or centrifugal geopolitics. They do not supply public goods. Loss of respect for elders, teachers and leaders marks the rot of social decency that its enlightenment culture clinches.

Educating the cognitive script of the constitution: The gamut of constitutional rights has provided Nepalis an opportunity to demand institutional resources of the state. The Constitution does not entitle people to demand the fulfillment of their rights from civil society, NGOs, business and political parties, as many of them are not members of these bodies but are familiar with their paternalistic and partisan style, rather than innovative and inclusive. If the Nepali constitution remains a contested site for political leaders and they come with dissimilar proposals for its reforms, people find every reason to question the motive of leaders. The deficits of constitutional enlightenment mean no common political socialisation of leaders.

In this sense, it is unlikely to satisfy social justice, normal life and heal wounds infected by diverse scales of violence. An unsteady psychological condition is only drying the soul, not refreshing hope, thus justifying the unfinished struggle of human will and purpose. Cognitive ability of people entails realizing their sovereignty and rights, tending to civic character and personality. Only then can they solve problems through the art of deliberation in the public sphere and compromise in mutual satisfaction, without the supremacy of legal quibbling, litigation, adversarial positions, or majority-decision practices by the adjudication system without the semblance of merit, justice and morality, thus affirming its popular adage about laws.

Access of invisible people to the institutional resource: So long as those deprived of political power and resources are satisfied with the national policies of the welfare state, they find no reason to become defiant and challenge the prerogative of the polity and its constitution through the eternal whirlpool of stirs. The psychological and economic bond of people with the state remains robust if Nepali leaders work to satisfy their vital needs and inspire their stake and support to democracy. It is not just the style of speechifying but the substance they deliver that stitches the trust and hope of Nepalis in governance. Ironically, the unconcern of most of Nepali leaders about the needs of the poor makes their position disconcerting. This means they must evolve an economic system that is ecologically sensitive, self-reliant and enables people to afford to pay adequate taxes to sustain the state’s autonomy in internal politics and sovereignty in the current of shifting geopolitics. Those policymakers who are quiet about the state of the nation and do not produce enlightened policies to improve it cannot be deemed wise and honest to the people expecting legitimate development dividends.

New learning: Artificial intelligence is creating a new opportunity for learning, teaching, writing, research and innovation. In politics, it has marked a shift from the art of leadership to lie, cheat and manipulate the consciousness of people through the presentation of doctored data of progress to a condition of post-truth where the psychology of emotion and feeling matters. Now social media plays a bigger role than formal agencies of socialisation such as families, educational institutions, political parties, civil society or religious bodies. Nepali scholars are now focusing more on age than gender, class, income disparity or region to analyse the sources of political acculturation and progress. Instrumental politics of age is, however, a risky strategy. It generates higher costs for those below and above Gen Z while benefits go to techo-mougals. In this sense, intellectual neutrality does not mean mediating quietly in the life of contemplation.

Enlightenment requires linking with the multi-generational people’s sense of judgment, use of conscience and conviction, learning from their experience and solving their problem beyond the habit-driven mode of careerism. Nepal has fallen seriously behind in progress and the means to produce it in a fair manner are slanted. Each regime following political change and elections, has evaded the opportunity to produce wealth for the future, remedy problems of eternal poverty, climate change and economic vices. The inequality of wealth across the social classes might sustain for generations to come unless a productive and distributive mechanism is placed for the wretched. Nepalis trusted their leaders to carry out the policies inscribed in the constitution but failed to break the cobweb of vested interests standing as barriers. There was no throb of sensitivity for long to the silent majority subjected to the reality of structural injustice, power politics and syndicate.

Youths’ vision

The future of the Nepali nation is built on its youths’ vision, zeal, courage, discipline and duty to the nation. The comfort zone of its paternalistic leaders, without any shred of enlightened commitment, failed to build a just society where all generations of Nepalis cherish shared sentiment and hope for a common future. But when the nation cannot control its politics, laws and policies, it is at the mercy of others and thus lacks self-confidence and dignity. Nepali youths must appreciate the sacrifices made by the ancestors on whose shoulders they stand as free citizens of a sovereign nation. They did not negotiate their dignity for a comfortable life but used strategy, enlightenment and courage for freedom.

Nepali leadership is responsible to change conditions by improving skills, knowledge and science and enthusing courage and character so that they can stand up against any thorny odds, including thought-conditioning by external agencies parroting: “Nepal is poor and daily becoming poorer.” Yet it has to stop canonizing the thieves of the state, corrupts and criminals for whom both popular sovereignty and state sovereignty are enemies and appreciate the public and organic intellectuals whose truthfulness and public voice bring the invisible to an upland light of enlightenment, justice, dignity and peace.

(Former Reader at the Department of Political Science, TU, Dahal writes on political and social issues.)
